title: HTML Basic Examples
summary: A small HTML page can have a heading, a paragraph, a link and a picture.
introduction: A small HTML page can have a heading, a paragraph, a link and a picture. Build the page one part at a time. Read the result after each change, just as you would check each step in a recipe.
learningObjectives: Recognise the six most common HTML elements at a glance
Predict what a short HTML snippet will render
Write comments that the browser ignores

blocks.text: HTML has six heading levels, `<h1>` to `<h6>`. `<h1>` is the main title of the page and should appear once; the others create sections and sub-sections.

Each `

` element is a block of text. Browsers add space between paragraphs automatically, and they collapse any extra spaces or line breaks inside your source into a single space.

blocks.text: The anchor element `<a>` creates a link. The `href` attribute holds the destination and the text between the tags is what the user clicks.

blocks.text: `` embeds an image. It has no closing tag. `src` points to the image file and `alt` describes it for people who cannot see it and for search engines. Setting `width` and `height` lets the browser reserve space before the image loads.
Use `<ul>` for an unordered (bulleted) list and `<ol>` for an ordered (numbered) list. Both contain `<li>` list items.
Anything between `<!--` and `-->` is a comment. Browsers ignore it, but anyone who views the source can read it, so never put secrets in comments.

blocks.code: Visible text

blocks.text: Comments are a good way to temporarily hide a block while you experiment, but remove stale commented-out code before you publish a page; it confuses the next person who reads it.
